title: Prototype and Pressure-Test the Plan (Lab)
summary: Students prototype their approved plan on the board, break it on purpose with a tricky curated input, and design an if-then fallback branch that keeps a person in the loop.
objectives: Prototype the prompt structure and pressure-test the plan against a tricky input.
Add a fallback branch for when the output fails a check.
Record what changed and why after the pressure test.

body: A plan on paper looks tidy. Today you find out how it behaves under pressure. You will build a quick prototype, then throw your hardest inputs at it on purpose - the missing item, the messy note, the two-in-one line. When it stumbles, you will not hide the failure; you will design a fallback branch that catches it safely. Engineers stress-test bridges before people cross them. You will stress-test your solution before it is trusted.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run my prompt structure on a normal input and read the output.
I can pressure-test it with a tricky input and spot where it fails.
I can add a fallback branch that says what to do when a check fails.
I can record the change I made and the reason for it.

terms.definition: A first working version built quickly to see how a design really behaves.
Deliberately trying a tricky input to reveal a weak spot.
An unusual input at the edge of what a solution expects, like a missing or double value.
A planned 'if a check fails, then...' response that handles a failure safely.
A label for what went wrong: wrong, unclear, or missing.

sections.heading: Prototype first, judge second
body: A [[prototype]] is a fast first version. Running it shows how your design behaves, not just how you hoped it would.
The teacher runs your prompt on the board with a normal curated input. You read the output and decide: did it meet the goal?

sections.heading: Design the fallback branch
body: When a check fails, a good solution follows a [[fallback branch]] instead of giving a confident wrong answer.
Write it as 'If the check fails, then ___ and ask a person.' Keeping a human in the loop is part of responsible design.
Remember: only curated, made-up inputs - never real names or personal data.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will prototype your approved plan, pressure-test it, and add a fallback branch. The teacher runs the AI on the board; you do not log in. Log every run.
items: Copy your prompt structure into the prototype slot of your log.
Watch the normal-input run on the board and record whether it met the goal.
Pressure-test with a tricky curated input and record the error type.
Write your fallback branch as an if-then sentence that asks a person.
Log the one change you made and the reason it will help.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which tricky input broke the most prototypes, and why?
Why is a handled failure safer than a confident wrong answer?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the weak spot your pressure test exposed.
Write how your fallback branch will handle it next week.

worksheet.title: Week 7 - Lab - Worksheet | Prototype and Pressure-Test the Plan (Lab)

questions.prompt: Predict then test: before the board run, predict how your prompt will handle one tricky input. After the run, record what actually happened.
questions.stem:
I predict the output will be ___.
The actual output was ___.
The error type was ___ (wrong / unclear / missing).
questions.lookFor: The prediction is written before the run and the actual output after it, and the error type is one of the three labels. A real pressure test exposes something - e.g. 'found: charger and a scarf' returning 'devices' only is a missing error, not a wrong one.

questions.prompt: Write your fallback branch: turn your exposed failure into a safe fallback using the if-then frame
questions.stem: If ___ then ___ and ask a person.
questions.lookFor: The branch handles the failure the pressure test actually exposed and keeps a person in the loop (e.g. 'if a notice names two items, then label each one separately, and if still unclear label it other and ask a person'). A vague branch, or one that does not match the observed failure, is only approaching.

questions.prompt: Prototype build/test log: record each run - the input used (curated), the output, whether it met the goal (Y/N), and the error type if any.
questions.lookFor: At least one normal run and one pressure test are logged, each with its curated input, the output, a Y/N against the goal, and a classified error type for any run that failed. Logs without an error type are returned.

questions.prompt: Exit ticket: write the weak spot you found and the fallback branch you designed for it.
questions.lookFor: Names one specific weak spot from their own log, not a general worry, and gives a fallback branch that visibly answers that weak spot.

questions.prompt: Challenge (stretch): design a second fallback for a different error type and say which failure is more likely and why.
questions.lookFor: A second branch aimed at a different error type (wrong / unclear / missing) from the first, plus a judgement about which failure is more likely with a reason drawn from the runs they logged.
